summary: This RFC describes generating a signed DNS response on demand for a nonexistent name by claiming the name exists but has no data for the queried type. Such responses need only one minimally covering NSEC or NSEC3 record, helping online signing servers reduce signing work.

eli5.summary: Asked about a page that doesn't exist, the server says "that name is here, but has nothing of that kind." This is cheaper to prove.

questions: what is compact denial of existence
how does dnssec prove a name does not exist
what is the compact answers ok flag
subtitle: How a DNSSEC server can prove a name does not exist by pretending it exists with no data, using one small signed record.

tldr.problem: Signing 'no such name' answers on the fly normally needs up to two signed NSEC records or up to three signed NSEC3 records, which costs bytes and cryptographic work and can leak zone contents.
tldr.mechanism: The server answers NOERROR with an empty answer (NODATA) and one signed NSEC or NSEC3 record that matches the queried name. A new synthetic type, NXNAME (128), in the type bitmap tells tools the name really does not exist.
tldr.outcome: Responses are smaller and cheaper to sign, but resolvers no longer see NXDOMAIN by default. An optional EDNS flag lets NXDOMAIN be restored.

facts.label: Response to a query for NXNAME

today: RFC 9824 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2025. It has not been obsoleted, and it updates RFC 4034 and RFC 4035 to allow the NXNAME pseudo-type in type bitmaps and NSEC records for names that do not exist in online signing.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
DNSSEC can give authenticated denial of existence: a signed proof that a DNS name or record type does not exist. Normally this uses signed NSEC or NSEC3 records. With online signing, a server computes those records on demand. A response for a nonexistent name needs up to two signed NSEC records or up to three signed NSEC3 records to show that the name was not in the zone and could not have come from a wildcard.

RFC 9824 describes Compact Denial of Existence (also called Compact Answers). The server claims the name exists but has no record sets of the queried type. That is a NODATA response: response code NOERROR with an empty answer section. It needs only one NSEC or NSEC3 record that matches the queried name.

Two advantages follow: the response is smaller, and less online cryptographic work is needed. Because the records are minimally covering, an adversary also cannot enumerate a zone by walking the NSEC chain or by running an offline dictionary attack on NSEC3 hashes.
sections.eli5: Instead of a long proof that something is missing, the server gives one short signed note that says 'this name is here, but it has nothing of that kind.'

sections.title: Telling Missing Names from Empty Ones with NXNAME
sections.content:
A NODATA answer has a problem: the type bitmap for a nonexistent name would hold only RRSIG and NSEC. An Empty Non-Terminal (ENT), a name with no records of its own but with names below it, has exactly the same bitmap, yet it does exist. Tools cannot tell the two apart.

The RFC defines NXNAME (type 128), a synthetic Meta-TYPE that signals a nonexistent name. It is added to the NSEC type bitmap next to RRSIG and NSEC. With NSEC3, it is the only entry in the bitmap. It stores no data in a zone and cannot be usefully queried.

Resolvers need no special handling for NXNAME. They may optionally use it to restore NXDOMAIN for applications, as described below.
sections.eli5: An empty folder in a filing cabinet and a folder that was never made look the same from the outside. NXNAME is a special sticker that says 'this folder was never made.'

sections.title: Generating Responses with NSEC
sections.content:
For a nonexistent name, the server returns NOERROR with an empty answer and a dynamically built NSEC record whose owner name matches the queried name. The Next Domain Name SHOULD be the immediate lexicographic successor, made by adding a leading label holding a single zero octet. The type bitmap MUST contain only RRSIG, NSEC and NXNAME, and the record MUST have RRSIGs.

For a name that exists but lacks the queried type, the NSEC record also matches the queried name and its bitmap lists the types that are present. For an ENT, the bitmap holds only RRSIG and NSEC.

For wildcard matches, the server signs the answer as though the name existed explicitly, so the RRSIG label count equals the number of labels in the query name minus the root label. That removes the need for an NSEC record proving no closer match. A wildcard NODATA match gets a single matching NSEC whose bitmap lists the types at the wildcard.

For unsigned referrals, the usual successor name would fall under the delegated subzone, so the Next Domain Name is formed by appending a zero octet to the first label of the owner name instead.

If a server receives an explicit query for the NXNAME type, it MUST return FORMERR. A resolver MUST NOT forward such queries upstream or attempt iterative resolution. The server MAY add Extended DNS Error code 30 (Invalid Query Type).
sections.eli5: When you ask about something that is not there, the server hands back one short signed card that names exactly what you asked about. A few special cases, like shortcuts and handoffs to other offices, get slightly different cards.

sections.title: NSEC3 and Response Code Restoration
sections.content:
NSEC3 is supported, though the RFC says there is no known advantage to using it here, since minimally covering NSEC already blocks zone enumeration. An existing NSEC3 online signer may still find it simpler to migrate. The NSEC3 parameters SHOULD be algorithm 1, flags 0, 0 additional iterations and an empty salt, written 1 0 0 -. The Next Hashed Owner Name is the binary hash plus one. For nonexistent names the bitmap holds only NXNAME, and for ENTs it is empty. No special form is needed for unsigned referrals.

Implementations should try to keep response code 3 (NXDOMAIN) where possible. For queries without the DO bit, servers could return a normal NXDOMAIN, but the RFC notes this has limited benefit because DNSSEC-aware recursive servers set the DO bit on outbound queries anyway. A validating resolver that understands NXNAME could change NOERROR to NXDOMAIN for downstream queriers that did not set DO.

An optional but recommended scheme adds a new EDNS0 header flag, Compact Answers OK (CO), in the second most significant bit of the flags field, right after DO. A resolver that sets CO accepts a NODATA response with a signed NXNAME and response code NXDOMAIN. The server then sets CO in its reply and sets the code to NXDOMAIN for nonexistent names. EDNS is hop-by-hop, so resolvers must record the flag in cache data and reset the code to NOERROR (0) for downstream queriers that did not set CO.
sections.eli5: Because the server now says 'found, but empty' instead of 'not found,' a special tick box lets an asker say 'it is okay to also tell me plainly that it is not found.'

sections.title: Operational Implications
sections.content:
For DNSSEC-enabled queries, a zone using Compact Answers never returns NXDOMAIN unless the optional restoration feature is implemented. Resolvers without that feature cannot return NXDOMAIN either. Tools that need to spot nonexistent names must look for NXNAME in the NSEC type bitmap.

Address lookup functions may do more work. A NODATA answer to an AAAA lookup can prompt another query for an A record at the same name, whereas NXDOMAIN could have suppressed it. This matters less for connection functions such as Happy Eyeballs, which send queries back to back.

Resolver optimizations that synthesize NXDOMAIN or wildcard answers, as in RFC 8020 and RFC 8198, cannot be used with responses of this kind. The RFC also notes that no online signing scheme with minimally covering NSEC or NSEC3 records permits that style of synthesis.
sections.eli5: Programs that expect a clear 'not found' answer may have to do extra checking, and helpful shortcuts that remember missing names no longer work.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Online signing means authoritative servers hold private signing keys, and exposing keys on Internet-reachable servers makes them easier to attack. Signing on demand is also heavier than returning precomputed signatures. Compact Answers reduce the number of signing operations compared with earlier techniques such as White Lies, but servers may still be more exposed to computational denial-of-service attacks. The RFC recommends signature algorithms with a comparatively low signing cost, such as those based on elliptic curves.

Some security tools read the response code to spot nonexistent names, and a NOERROR code affects them. The DNS header is not cryptographically protected, so the response code cannot be authenticated; inferring status from signed data in the body, such as NXNAME, is actually more secure.

Since resolvers cannot do aggressive negative caching, Pseudorandom Subdomain Attacks become more effective. Random names must all be passed to the domain's authoritative servers, which makes resource exhaustion more likely if they cannot absorb the load. Operators who do not need the size and cost savings can choose conventional online signing or precomputed signatures.
sections.eli5: The server has to keep its signing pen close at hand, which is risky, and bad guys can ask about lots of made-up names to tire it out.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA allocated three code points. NXNAME is RR type 128, taken from the Meta-TYPE range. A lower number in that range keeps the type bitmap, and so the response, smaller. The EDNS header flag CO (Compact Answers OK) is bit 1. Extended DNS Error code 30, Invalid Query Type, is generally applicable to any RR type that ought not to appear in queries.

Appendix A and B record history: before type 128, deployments used other ways to tell missing names from ENTs, and private type codes 65281 and 65238 were used by some operators before the official code point.
sections.eli5: The official list of numbers got three new entries: one for the special sticker, one for the tick box and one for a new kind of error message.

data.title: Generated NSEC examples
data.code:
; nonexistent name a.example.com.
a.example.com. 300 IN NSEC \000.a.example.com. RRSIG NSEC NXNAME

; referral to unsigned subzone
sub.example.com. 300 IN NSEC sub\000.example.com. NS RRSIG NSEC
